Teaching Agents to Code Reliably

Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin ††thanks: Work done during an internship at AWS AI Labs. Affiliation: Stanford University Email: muahmed@stanford.edu    Myeongsoo Kim    Kangrui Ruan    Shweta Garg    Varun Kumar    Murali Krishna Ramanathan Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Affiliation: {mysoo, kangruir, shwegarg, kuvrun, mkraman}@amazon.com

1 Introduction

Autonomous coding agents resolve repository issues through code inspection, editing, and test execution (Jimenez et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024). Repeated attempts and verification can improve resolution by increasing inference-time computation (Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2024; Han et al., 2026). Their benefit depends on whether additional attempts produce correct repairs and whether the agent can identify them. Attempts can revisit the same edit location or repeat an incorrect repair. A test generated by the agent can share the patch’s mistaken interpretation of the issue and accept incorrect behavior (Ahmed et al., 2025). More candidates do not guarantee a correct selected patch.

We distinguish candidate coverage from selection quality. Coverage is the fraction of issues for which the candidate set contains at least one correct repair. Selection quality is the fraction of those issues for which the agent returns a correct candidate. Oracle pass@88 measures coverage across eight attempts, whereas the accuracy of the selected patch depends on both quantities. Verification also guides the search by determining whether the agent revises a patch, explores another location, or stops. The verifier therefore affects both the candidates generated and the patch returned.

We hypothesize that training can improve repair search and test discrimination under a fixed backbone and scaffold. Our diagnostic study examines edit locations, repair approaches, and verification decisions on SWE-bench Verified. Repeated self-verification produces few changes to the submitted patches, while different problem-solving preambles produce complementary repairs. Proactive localization visits more locations than reactive search but resolves fewer issues (Section 2.1). These observations motivate training the agent to use execution feedback when choosing its next edit and to evaluate tests by their ability to detect incorrect repairs. Execution provides evidence beyond the agent’s judgment of its own output (Huang et al., 2024).

Our approach combines a test-time diagnostic with two training stages. The diagnostic pairs exploration of edit locations and repair approaches with differential verification, which runs a reproduction on the patched and reverted repository. Weighted supervised fine-tuning uses the resulting trajectories, with weights determined by repair-quality tier, exploration score, and agent-step count. Reinforcement learning then evaluates generated tests against oracle-rejected patch variants and sibling repairs. On the 270270 SWE-bench Verified issues held out from SFT and RL training, the two training stages raise greedy pass@11 from 31.9%31.9\% to 43.0%43.0\% (Table 7). Across eight attempts, oracle coverage rises from 46.7%46.7\% to 60.7%60.7\% and selected-patch accuracy from 33.5%33.5\% to 50.5%50.5\%, with selection efficiency increasing from 0.720.72 to 0.830.83 (Table 3). These measurements separate improvements in candidate coverage from improvements in selection. On the external benchmarks, RL raises pass@11 over SFT from 15.7%15.7\% to 20.2%20.2\% on SWE-bench Pro and from 24.2%24.2\% to 31.8%31.8\% on SWE-PolyBench, while DeepSWE full resolution remains zero at this scale, though its partial-credit measures rise (Table 6).

2 Methodology

This section describes the test-time search procedures, weighted trajectory supervision, and reinforcement learning objective. Figure 1 illustrates exploration and verification within one repair trajectory.

2.1 Test-Time Scaling Methods on Coding Agents

The diagnostic uses all 500500 SWE-bench Verified issues to analyze repair and verification failures. We select 230230 issues from this population for training dataset curation and hold the remaining 270270 out of SFT and RL training. All search procedures run on the same backbone and scaffold. Table 1 reports resolution, agent-steps, attempts per instance, and diversity. Attempt limits and stopping rules differ by procedure, so each comparison reflects an accuracy and cost trade-off.

We compare single attempts, repeated self-verification, eight repair preambles, proactive localization, and reactive bans on failed edits or locations. The preambles reach an oracle union of 305/500305/500 issues, while repeated self-verification leaves 7878 to 85%85\% of audit passes without a code change. Appendix A.1 describes the procedures and scoring rules.

Differential-verification search pairs up to eight locations and repair approaches. It runs each reproduction on the patched and reverted trees, checks repository tests and changed-line execution, and uses the resulting score to stop or prune search. A reproduction that passes on both trees receives zero credit. Search uses repository execution rather than hidden grader feedback. It resolves 52.8%52.8\% of issues against 46.8%46.8\% for the eight-sample control, using 48.1%48.1\% of its agent-steps (Table 1). Appendix B.11 reports component ablations.

2.2 Supervised Fine-Tuning on Weighted Agent Trajectories

We train the policy to imitate repair trajectories weighted by outcome quality, exploration, and agent-step count. The training interface matches the inference interface. Some examples rely on verifier outcomes rather than gold labels, so the corpus can contain incorrect repairs.

Corpus construction.

We curate the SFT corpus from the 230230 issues selected after the all-500500 failure analysis in Section 2.1. Trajectories from the remaining 270270 issues are excluded from SFT and RL training. The corpus includes the six search procedures in Table 1 and the methodology-diversity runs, generated with Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct under mini-SWE-agent. Each example records the conversation, final patch, edit locations, agent-step count, verifier outcome, available gold label, and behavior tags. Trajectories are ranked within each instance_id by the weight defined below, with ties resolved by fewer steps. The retained corpus contains 5,0615{,}061 examples from 230230 issues.

The corpus includes contrastive-edit examples pairing a correct repair with an incorrect candidate at the same location, and reproduction examples distinguishing buggy from fixed behavior. Contrastive examples receive additional weight when the incorrect candidate passed the verifier. These examples are included in the 5,0615{,}061 total.

Quality tiers.

Each example receives the weight of the first tier it matches. Tier T​1T1 has weight 1.01.0 and requires a gold-resolved patch that was selected or received a verifier score of at least 1.01.0. Tier T​2T2 has weight 0.60.6 and requires either a verifier score of at least 1.01.0 or a gold-resolved patch with a verifier pass. Tier T​3T3 has weight 0.250.25 and requires a non-empty patch with a weaker positive verifier signal. All remaining examples receive weight 00. Only T​1T1 requires a gold label.

Exploration and efficiency weights.

We multiply the tier weight by exploration and efficiency factors.

w=wtier⏟quality⋅(1+λ​ν~)⏟exploration⋅(1+β⁡[1−min⁡(1,stepsSref)])⏟efficiency,λ=1.0,β=0.5,Sref=120.w\;=\;\underbrace{w_{\text{tier}}}_{\text{quality}}\cdot\underbrace{\bigl(1+\lambda\,\tilde{\nu}\bigr)}_{\text{exploration}}\cdot\underbrace{\Bigl(1+\beta\bigl[1-\min(1,\tfrac{\text{steps}}{S_{\text{ref}}})\bigr]\Bigr)}_{\text{efficiency}},\qquad\lambda=1.0,\ \beta=0.5,\ S_{\text{ref}}=120. (1)

The effective novelty score ν~\tilde{\nu} has behavior-dependent floors of 0.60.6 for post-ban recovery and self-correction, 0.50.5 for localization-win and synthesis-only solves, and 0.40.4 for methodology-unique solves. The efficiency factor decreases from 1.51.5 at zero steps to 1.01.0 at Sref=120S_{\text{ref}}=120 steps and remains 1.01.0 for longer trajectories. These factors adjust the contribution of each example to supervised training.

2.3 Reinforcement Learning for Discriminative Verification

The SFT objective imitates trajectories without ever rewarding a test for rejecting an incorrect repair (Shum et al., 2025). We add a reinforcement objective that evaluates generated tests against incorrect programs, which measures which incorrect behaviors a test detects.

Generated objects.

For each training issue, the policy produces a patch PP and a test TT containing assertions {a1,…,an}\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\}. We draw kk rollouts per issue. The other k−1k-1 patches in the group are sibling repairs, which provide additional candidates for test evaluation. A gold execution oracle 𝒢\mathcal{G} determines whether a patch satisfies the training issue’s evaluation tests.

Oracle access and rollout feedback.

The policy observes repository files, command results, and the pytest output of TT on PP. Revision rounds return surviving patch variants as counterexamples that the policy can use to revise its patch or test. The policy does not receive gold tests, gold verdicts, assertion-credit scores, or group advantages. Oracle labels are used by the scoring procedure described below. The completed rollout receives a scalar reward, from which we compute trajectory and assertion-token advantages for the training update.

Mutation evaluation.

The harness generates variants from the current patch using deterministic operators and a frozen model distinct from the policy. The operators cover boundary, value, logic, control-flow, and effect faults. Model-generated variants are produced during the run rather than retrieved from a cache. A line trace checks that the test executes the patched lines. A variant counts as detected when an assertion fails. Uncaught errors receive no detection credit.

The scoring set SS contains oracle-rejected variants and oracle-rejected sibling repairs. Candidates that pass the gold tests are excluded from this negative set. Passing the gold tests does not establish semantic equivalence, but it prevents those candidates from being scored as known incorrect repairs. We record the detected subset as Kill⁡(T)\mathrm{Kill}(T). Appendix A.6 gives a worked example.

The repair loop allows up to three revision rounds and applies a penalty for additional rounds. Exploration terms measure group diversity across edited files and assertion targets, coverage of fault classes, and repetition of test templates. These terms supplement the patch-correctness and test-discrimination signals.

Post-rollout reward.

We score each completed rollout with

Rtraj=wc​Correct+wv​Verif+we​Edit+wp​Process,R_{\text{traj}}\;=\;w_{c}\,\textsc{Correct}\;+\;w_{v}\,\textsc{Verif}\;+\;w_{e}\,\textsc{Edit}\;+\;w_{p}\,\textsc{Process}, (2)

We use wc=3.0w_{c}=3.0, wv=1.0w_{v}=1.0, we=0.4w_{e}=0.4, and wp=0.2w_{p}=0.2. The correctness term is 11 when PP satisfies 𝒢\mathcal{G} and 00 otherwise. The verification term measures detection of the scored negatives and agreement with the oracle.

Verif=|Kill⁡(T)||S|⏟dense slope+λfp 1[Kill(T)=S]⏟fixpoint bonus+h⁡(T)⏟honesty\textsc{Verif}\;=\;\underbrace{\tfrac{|\mathrm{Kill}(T)|}{|S|}}_{\text{dense slope}}\;+\;\underbrace{\lambda_{\text{fp}}\,\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{Kill}(T)=S]}_{\text{fixpoint bonus}}\;+\;\underbrace{h(T)}_{\text{honesty}} (3)

The detection fraction provides partial credit, and λfp=0.5\lambda_{\text{fp}}=0.5 adds a bonus when the test detects every variant in SS. The agreement term h⁡(T)h(T) is −0.5-0.5 for false acceptance, −0.25-0.25 for false rejection, and 00 when the test verdict agrees with the oracle. The resulting verification term lies in [−0.5,1.5][-0.5,1.5]. The edit-placement and reproduce-first terms lie in [0,1][0,1] and contribute only when Verif>0\textsc{Verif}>0 or Correct=1\textsc{Correct}=1.

The weighted auxiliary terms have a combined range of at most 2.62.6, below the correctness weight of 3.03.0. Every correct rollout therefore receives a higher scalar reward than every incorrect rollout. The auxiliary terms determine the ordering within each correctness class. This ordering concerns the scalar reward, not the sign of every group-relative advantage.

Detecting all scored variants does not establish correctness beyond that set. For a fixed test and MM independent draws from a fixed mutant distribution with no survivors, the one-sided 95%95\% upper confidence bound on the survival probability is ρ≤1−0.051/M\rho\leq 1-0.05^{1/M}. Table 17 reports training completion and held-out detection. Appendix A.4 specifies empty negative sets, invalid executions, and other boundary cases.

Assertion credit.

We optimize with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards normalized within each issue’s rollout group give the trajectory advantage AtrajA_{\text{traj}}. The kill matrix Km,iK_{m,i} records whether assertion ii detects mutant mm. We allocate credit to detecting assertions using

c~i=∑m:Km,i=1ωcls​(m)κm,ci=c~i∑jc~j\tilde{c}_{i}\;=\;\sum_{m:\,K_{m,i}=1}\frac{\omega_{\text{cls}(m)}}{\kappa_{m}},\qquad c_{i}\;=\;\frac{\tilde{c}_{i}}{\sum_{j}\tilde{c}_{j}} (4)

Here, κm\kappa_{m} is the number of assertions that detect mutant mm, and ωcls​(m)\omega_{\text{cls}(m)} is its fault-class weight. Each detected mutant divides one class-weighted unit among its detecting assertions. Normalization gives cic_{i}. We set st=ci⁡(t)s_{t}=c_{i(t)} for tokens in assertion i⁡(t)i(t) and st=0s_{t}=0 elsewhere. The token advantage is

At=Atraj+β​G​Atraj+​st,Atraj+=max⁡(Atraj,0),G∈{0,1}A_{t}\;=\;A_{\text{traj}}\;+\;\beta\,G\,A_{\text{traj}}^{+}\,s_{t},\qquad A_{\text{traj}}^{+}=\max(A_{\text{traj}},0),\quad G\in\{0,1\} (5)

The gate G=1G=1 when the patch resolves the issue or the test detects every scored mutant. The assertion bonus is applied when this gate is satisfied and Atraj>0A_{\text{traj}}>0. Complete detection can therefore enable assertion credit for an incorrect patch. The bonus rewards detection of scored negatives and does not certify the accompanying patch. The trajectory-level agreement term penalizes false rejection, but the unsigned assertion credit contains no penalty for rejecting correct alternatives. Patch tokens retain the trajectory advantage. Setting β=0\beta=0 removes the assertion bonus.

The unnormalized credit c~i\tilde{c}_{i} is the Shapley allocation of a weighted coverage game in which an assertion set receives the total weight of the mutants it detects. This interpretation describes the credit allocation and provides no convergence guarantee. Appendix A.4 discusses assertion execution and token-span mapping. We use GRPO group size k=6k=6, PPO clip 0.20.2, and no KL penalty. Appendix B.5 lists the training settings.

3 Evaluation

3.1 Evaluation Protocol

Populations and exposure.

Section 2.1 analyzes all 500500 SWE-bench Verified issues. We curate SFT and RL data from 230230 of them and evaluate the trained policies on the remaining 270270, of which 180180 come from training repositories and 9090 from repositories excluded from training. Held-out means excluded from SFT and RL training. All 270270 appeared in the diagnostic, so this split measures held-out issues within a benchmark used for method development rather than an out-of-distribution evaluation. Transfer uses DeepSWE (113113 tasks), SWE-PolyBench, SWE-bench Lite, and SWE-bench Pro (731731 issues). The 3030B study evaluates all four after SFT and all but Lite after RL, while the 77B and 1414B runs also evaluate Lite (Appendix A.8).

Decoding and aggregation.

The policies share the backbone, scaffold, tools, context limits, and attempt budget. Pass@11 uses the greedy first attempt, and eight-attempt evaluation adds seven samples at T=0.7T=0.7, so the samples are not identically distributed. This budget differs from the eight methodology-conditioned chains and the candidate grid of Section 2.1. The configuration specifies three seeds.

Candidate populations and metrics.

Coverage and selection use each policy’s own eight-candidate sets. Verifier discrimination instead uses one frozen bank of labeled repairs per held-out issue, shared across policies, combining natural incorrect repairs from several generators with correct alternatives, with labels withheld from the test-generating policy. Cross-error-source evaluation separates familiar operators, held-out operators, an excluded semantic-mutant generator, and natural incorrect repairs. Repair correctness is defined by the benchmark grader, so resolution and verifier labels measure agreement with its tests rather than semantic correctness. Pass@88 is oracle coverage, Selected@88 is the fraction whose selected candidate is correct, and selection efficiency is Selected@88/pass@88. Taking a correct repair as the positive class, precision is T​P/(T​P+F​P)TP/(TP+FP), the false-positive rate is F​P/(F​P+T​N)FP/(FP+TN), correct acceptance is T​P/(T​P+F​N)TP/(TP+FN), and balanced accuracy averages correct acceptance and incorrect rejection. DeepSWE verifier labels use fail-to-pass satisfaction. We report ηk=Ukloc/k\eta_{k}=U_{k}^{\mathrm{loc}}/k as location diversity per attempt, and agent-steps count agent interactions rather than tokens or execution time. Appendix B.9 defines acceptance coverage, correct-alternative acceptance, and the zero-survivor audit.

3.2 Repair Accuracy

On the Verified split held out from training, SFT increases pass@11 from 31.9%31.9\% to 35.2%35.2\% and RL from SFT raises it to 43.0%43.0\% (Table 5). Applying the same RL objective to the base policy yields 35.9%35.9\% (Table 7), so the objective gains 4.04.0 points from the base policy and 7.87.8 from the supervised one.

3.3 Candidate Coverage and Selection

SFT increases oracle pass@88 from 46.7%46.7\% to 51.1%51.1\%, while RL raises it to 60.7%60.7\%. Selected@88 increases from 33.5%33.5\% to 38.5%38.5\% after SFT and to 50.5%50.5\% after RL. Selection efficiency rises from 0.720.72 to 0.750.75 and then to 0.830.83 (Table 3). The gains therefore involve both the availability of correct repairs and the fraction selected by the verifier. The coverage half traces to the exploratory behavior the corpus weighting teaches. Trained to spread attempts across locations and vary the edit, the policy reaches 1.981.98 distinct localizations per issue against 1.411.41 for the base model, and the share of samples contributing a new fault location rises from 0.180.18 to 0.250.25 at eight attempts, so more of the budget lands on ground no earlier sample covered.

Behavioral changes under supervision.

Supervision raises pass@11 on every suite that resolves any task, by 3.33.3 points on Verified and 3.83.8, 8.48.4, and 13.413.4 on SWE-PolyBench, Lite, and Pro (Table 2). The trajectory measures move in the same direction on every suite, with more files read before the first edit, smaller patches, fewer test-file edits, and fewer steps to first submission. Reproduce-first is the one measure where base leads, 94.4%94.4\% against 92.1%92.1\% on Verified, while rising on all four transfer suites. This is the behavior the weighting targets. A policy that commits to one site keeps editing it, so a wrong first localization is unrecoverable, and Section 2.1 showed that breadth alone loses to blind retry. The weighting rewards moving on once execution rules a site out, so the added breadth lands where feedback directs it rather than across arbitrary sites. At matched corpus and budget, removing the exploration factor lowers distinct localizations from 1.981.98 to 1.741.74 and pass@11 from 35.2%35.2\% to 34.8%34.8\% on Verified, and from 4.134.13 to 3.703.70 and 24.2%24.2\% to 23.2%23.2\% on SWE-PolyBench (Table B.10). Staging the terms raises localization and resolution together, from 1.551.55 and 33.7%33.7\% under uniform weighting to 1.901.90 and 34.8%34.8\% with exploration, while an interface-compliance control reaches 1.451.45 and 32.6%32.6\%, below uniform on both (Table 19). Which trajectory measure carries the effect is not separated.

Steps to first submission decrease from 62.562.5 to 56.056.0 (Table 2), and η8\eta_{8} rises from 0.340.34 to 0.610.61 on DeepSWE. Location diversity does not measure candidate correctness, so it complements rather than replaces the coverage analysis.

3.4 Verifier Discrimination on Fixed Candidates

On one frozen candidate bank shared across policies, so that differences reflect the verifier and not an easier candidate population, the RL verifier rejects 87.4%87.4\% of incorrect repairs against 73.0%73.0\% for SFT, while correct-patch acceptance and balanced accuracy rise with it, so both sides of the decision improve rather than the verifier becoming uniformly stricter. Correctness-only RL captures roughly a third of that gain (Table 4). The per-assertion credit pushes the test toward assertions that each catch something the others miss, since a detected variant divides one unit among its detectors and a redundant assertion collects less than a new one. Two mutant sources keep that pressure from collapsing onto one distribution, since an assertion set tuned to operator shapes leaves model-generated variants alive. Training on operators alone loses pass@11, precision, and zero-survivor rate together (Table 9), and rejection degrades gradually off the training distribution (Table 16).

The verification code itself changes. The median test carries no assertions before training and 1111 after, length falls from 4242 to 3333 lines, and it covers 33 of 55 fault classes rather than none (Table 7). A test with no assertions cannot reject any variant.

Holding the base repair generator fixed, replacing its verifier with the trained verifier raises resolution from 31.9%31.9\% to 36.5%36.5\% (Table 15). The estimated interaction between changing the generator and changing the verifier is −0.1-0.1 percentage points, with a 95%95\% confidence interval of [−2.6,2.4][-2.6,2.4]. This experiment detects a verifier contribution without establishing a nonzero interaction.

Figure 2 reports a layer-wise probe comparison. The post-RL curve has higher AUC, with its largest differences in the mid-to-late layers. This association does not establish a causal contribution to repair accuracy.

3.5 Reward Controls

The RL controls start from one SFT checkpoint and match training issues, update counts, and rollout budgets. Correctness-only GRPO reaches 39.6%39.6\% pass@11 and 28.5%28.5\% verifier precision. Adding scalar verification reward raises these values to 40.7%40.7\% and 38.4%38.4\%. Assertion credit raises them to 43.0%43.0\% and 41.7%41.7\% (Table 5b). Both the verification reward and assertion credit contribute to the reported gain.

Uniform assertion credit yields 38.0%38.0\% precision and shuffling it at matched total mass yields 31.5%31.5\%, so placement affects discrimination beyond the amount assigned. Removing mutation evaluation reduces pass@11 from 43.0%43.0\% to 38.1%38.1\%, the largest reduction among the component removals in Table 8. Allowing uncaught errors to count as detections reduces it to 39.6%39.6\%. These removals measure contributions within the full configuration and need not have additive effects. Ungating the shaping terms costs 1.91.9 points, removing the repair loop costs 3.03.0 while leaving precision at 40.1%40.1\%, and removing the exploration terms costs 1.51.5 (Table 8).

Group size raises both metrics, from 41.5%41.5\% pass@11 and 39.0%39.0\% precision at k=4k{=}4 to 43.0%43.0\% and 41.7%41.7\% at the trained k=6k{=}6 and 43.3%43.3\% and 42.6%42.6\% at k=16k{=}16. Lowering the correctness weight raises precision to 43.2%43.2\% while pass@11 falls to 38.9%38.9\% (Table 10), so the two respond differently to the same reward change.

3.6 Transfer and Limitations

RL improves pass@11 over SFT by 8.38.3 percentage points on train-exposed issues, 7.77.7 on test issues from training repositories, and 7.87.8 on repositories excluded from training, reaching 45.7%45.7\%, 44.4%44.4\%, and 40.0%40.0\% respectively (Table 5a). The gain is near-constant across the exposure gradient while the absolute level falls, the pattern expected if the objective transfers rather than recalling training fixes. On SWE-PolyBench, pass@11 increases from 24.2%24.2\% to 31.8%31.8\%. On SWE-bench Pro, it increases from 15.7%15.7\% to 20.2%20.2\% (Table 6). These evaluations support transfer beyond the training issues. They do not exclude pretraining exposure to public repositories.

DeepSWE full resolution remains zero at this model scale, but its internal measures improve. SFT raises the tasks with at least one satisfied fail-to-pass test from 1717 to 2121 of 113113 and the mean best-of-eight satisfied fraction from 4.0%4.0\% to 4.8%4.8\% (Table 13), which is partial test satisfaction rather than completed repair. Verifier precision uses a different positive criterion here (Section 3.1).

The signed assertion-credit ablation raises correct-alternative acceptance from 78.0%78.0\% to 84.0%84.0\%, cross-generator discrimination from 74.0%74.0\% to 78.0%78.0\%, and pass@11 from 43.0%43.0\% to 43.3%43.3\% (Table 18). This result supports adding an assertion-level penalty for false rejection. The main results use unsigned credit, so the signed variant’s gains apply to this ablation.

Verification remains sensitive to the source of incorrect repairs. The RL verifier rejects 91.0%91.0\% of familiar-operator mutants, 84.0%84.0\% of held-out operators, 79.0%79.0\% of variants from an excluded generator, and 74.0%74.0\% of natural incorrect repairs from independent generators. The latter exceeds SFT by 1212 percentage points, while correct-alternative acceptance remains 78.0%78.0\% (Table 16). Complete detection of a finite mutant set does not establish correctness outside that set.

The 77B and 1414B experiments gain from both stages. Verified pass@88 rises 21.9→30.4→33.3%21.9\to 30.4\to 33.3\% at 77B and 27.0→36.7→42.6%27.0\to 36.7\to 42.6\% at 1414B, and SWE-PolyBench rises 8.0→17.8%8.0\to 17.8\% and 19.8→37.4%19.8\to 37.4\% (Table 14). Published coder results in Appendix A.5 provide context but use different scaffolds, subsets, or selection protocols. They do not constitute matched comparisons. Agent-step savings also exclude differences in token lengths and test-execution costs.

4 Related Work

Repository search and feedback.

SWE-agent and OpenHands provide interfaces for repository inspection, editing, and execution (Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024). Agentless organizes repair around localization (Xia et al., 2024), and inference-time scaling studies examine additional attempts (Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2024). Our diagnostic holds backbone and scaffold fixed and compares how location search and verification affect repair. Generated tests also support candidate selection (Chen et al., 2023), and we measure candidate coverage and selected accuracy as distinct outcomes.

Training repair and test generation.

CodeRL trains code generation from execution feedback (Le et al., 2022), SWE-Gym studies training repository agents and verifiers (Pan et al., 2024), and CURE co-trains a coder and unit tester with reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2025b). Our policy generates both the patch and its test, and the reward combines patch correctness with detection of oracle-rejected variants. SWT-Bench evaluates tests for repository bug fixes (Mündler et al., 2024), a related setting for assessing tests beyond whether they execute.

Mutation rewards and credit assignment.

MIST-RL rewards each test for detecting mutants earlier tests missed and penalizes redundancy (Zhu et al., 2026). Ockhamareto is the closest comparator for our token-level credit, mapping mutation contributions to test-block tokens under a Pareto gate on suite effectiveness and size (Huang et al., 2026). Our credit divides each detected mutant’s weight among its detecting assertions and applies a positive-advantage bonus gated by repair correctness or complete detection, with the trajectory reward prioritizing repair correctness. These differences concern the reward and credit rule rather than introducing mutation testing or token-level attribution.

Test and patch revision.

CoHarden generates a reproduction before editing and uses mutant-based feedback to revise tests and fixes (Tan et al., 2026), the closest comparison to our revision loop. We also train the policy from those signals and evaluate the resulting verifier on frozen candidates, correct alternatives, and incorrect repairs from independent generators.

5 Conclusion

We hypothesized that reliable repair rests on three learnable behaviors, locating the fault, varying the edit, and verifying which candidate to return. The first two determine candidate coverage and the third selection quality, neither compensating for the other, and the swap estimates their contributions as additive. Weighted supervision and mutation-based reinforcement learning improve both, with gains on SWE-bench Pro and SWE-PolyBench and, on DeepSWE, partial credit without full resolution. The constraint is general, since a proposer scoring its own work cannot be wrong, so negatives must be manufactured rather than collected.

Where the verifier is weakest indicates what to improve. Rejection falls from 91.0%91.0\% on familiar operators to 74.0%74.0\% on repairs from independent generators, so a wider negative distribution during training is the first direction. The second is the signed credit rule, which charges an assertion for rejecting a correct alternative and raises correct-alternative acceptance from 78.0%78.0\% to 84.0%84.0\% in our ablation, though not yet under the full evaluation. Folding the verifier into the search loop, so that it steers exploration rather than filtering afterwards, would reach the coverage limit selection cannot.

Appendix A Appendix

This appendix provides reward ablations, implementation details, comparator studies, and a worked reward example. It also reports transfer and model-scale results and documents the prompts, search logic, and experiment configurations.

A.1 Test-time search procedures

Self-verification. The agent submits a patch, then runs up to three audit passes that read the repository, run tests, and revise, with no grader feedback (prompt in Appendix B.12). It resolves 184/500184/500 (36.8%36.8\%) at 189,371189{,}371 agent-steps (1,0291{,}029 per solve), yet 7878 to 85%85\% of audit passes change no code and across four attempts it reaches only 1.101.10 distinct locations and 1.311.31 distinct edits. It neither escapes its wrong first guess nor stops paying to re-examine it, taking both the lowest accuracy and the highest cost.

Single-axis diagnosis. One attempt per issue, no retry and no diversity mechanism, fixing the single-sample reference the other procedures answer to. It resolves 189/500189/500 (37.8%37.8\%) at 41,33241{,}332 agent-steps, the cheapest run in the study at 219219 steps per solve.

Methodology diversity. Running each issue under eight problem-solving preambles (Appendix B.13) solves overlapping but distinct subsets, with combined oracle coverage 305/500305/500 (61.0%61.0\%), above any single preamble. This label-using union is not a deployable rule, yet it marks the headroom. The agent already produces a correct fix for far more issues than one strategy surfaces, so selection limits performance more than generation.

Directed exploration. Up-front localization pins one attempt to each of 2.462.46 ranked sites yet resolves only 210/500210/500 (42.0%42.0\%), below blind retries (213/500213/500), so broad coverage alone does not help. Spending attempts on the right sites does, and that needs execution feedback. Banning a confirmed-wrong edit signature and stopping on a strong positive resolves 217/500217/500 (43.4%43.4\%) at 131,417131{,}417 steps, reaching 1.841.84 locations and 2.792.79 edits with early stops on 6565 issues.

Reactive location diversity. Banning the whole location, its files and functions, resolves 225/500225/500 (45.0%45.0\%) at 585585 steps per solve, under the ban and early-stop rules of Appendix B.14. Location diversity pays only when earned reactively, and reactive location-banning (225225) exceeds reactive edit-banning (217217), blind retries (213213), and proactive site-planning (210210), in that order.

Differential-verification search. The combined procedure builds up to eight candidate cells, each pairing one localization with one repair approach. It scores every candidate by executing the agent’s own reproduction twice, once on the tree carrying the patch and once on that same tree with the patch reverted. A failure on the reverted tree together with a pass on the patched tree shows the patch changed the behavior the reproduction measures, which is weaker than showing the patch correct elsewhere. The score itself rises with how much independent evidence stands behind that verdict, and it decides whether search continues. A confirmed differential scores 1.21.2 when two further checks agree, the repository’s existing tests still pass and the reproduction touches the changed lines, and 1.01.0 when either is missing, which reads a regression failure as pre-existing rather than caused by the patch. A patch whose reproduction passes while the reverted run returns no verdict scores 0.30.3, since the pass is real but nothing corroborates it. No usable signal or a broken harness scores 00. A vacuous differential, where the reproduction passes on both trees, means it never exercised the fault, so the candidate takes a hard 00 and the location is pruned. Any score of at least 1.01.0 is strong enough to stop the search. Every decision uses the agent’s own reproduction and the repository tests, never the hidden grader.

Differential-verification search resolves 264/500264/500 (52.8%52.8\%) against 234/500234/500 (46.8%46.8\%) for the eight-sample control, at 132,697132{,}697 agent-steps, 48.1%48.1\% of the control’s 275,943275{,}943, and 3.123.12 attempts per issue. That is 503503 steps per solve against 1,1791{,}179. Early stopping fires on about 102102 issues and pruning drops 126126 localizations across 7373 issues, so the gains come from spending compute where feedback says it will pay. A component ablation (Appendix B.11) isolates each part. Dropping the two-tree differential does the most damage (52.8→47.4%52.8\to 47.4\%, near the eight-sample baseline), while early stopping costs compute alone (steps/solve 503→728503\to 728 at unchanged resolution).

A.2 Reinforcement learning results by starting point

The reinforcement objective is applied twice, once to the base policy and once to the supervised policy, so that the contribution of the initialization can be read off directly. Both starting points improve on every metric in Table 7, which shows the objective does not depend on supervision to function. The size of the gain does depend on it. Pass@11 rises by 4.04.0 points from the base policy and by 7.87.8 from the supervised one, and verifier precision by 9.69.6 against 14.914.9 points, so the same reward is worth roughly twice as much once the policy already searches widely. The reason is visible in how GRPO forms its advantage, since rollouts that repeat the same edit share the same outcome and leave the group-relative advantage flat, while a wider candidate set puts correct and incorrect patches in the same group and gives the verifier term something to separate. Table 4 scores the resulting verifiers on one shared bank of labeled repairs, which removes the possibility that the improvement reflects an easier candidate population rather than a better verifier.

A.3 Reinforcement Learning Ablations

Each ablation removes or varies one component of the objective or training configuration described in Section 2.3. Unless otherwise noted, runs start from the supervised policy and are evaluated on SWE-bench Verified. We report the issue resolution rate (pass@11) and verifier precision against gold correctness labels. Table 9 varies the adversary that generates the semantic mutants, and Table 10 sweeps the reward weights and the group size.

A.4 RL objective implementation details and boundary cases

Two implementation notes accompany the per-assertion credit of Eq. 4. Mapping st=cis_{t}=c_{i} onto every token of assertion ii scales its total bonus by the span length LiL_{i}, so a per-token form st=ci/Lis_{t}=c_{i}/L_{i} removes this length effect. And ordinary execution halts a test at its first failing assertion, so reconstructing the full matrix KK needs isolated, independently executable test nodes. The Shapley reading of c~i\tilde{c}_{i} carries no convergence claim.

We define the scored quantities only when their inputs exist and fix the empty cases explicitly. With no valid negatives (|S|=0|S|=0) the kill fraction is undefined and the fixpoint bonus does not fire, so we record insufficient negatives and give no verifier credit. With no assertions or no detected mutants we zero the local credit cic_{i} and log the event. Infrastructure or import errors count as invalid execution and earn no behavioral-kill credit, so a broken harness earns no reward. The honesty term penalizes a test that fails on a correct repair, so an always-failing test cannot look discriminative. We report and control the valid mutant count and duplicate rate, since zero-survivor rates are otherwise incomparable. The gate GG is an OR, so the local bonus can fire on a resolved or complete rollout, correctness still enters only through Correct, and we never read a full kill as correctness assurance.

Table 11 lists published results with their backbones, scaffolds, and evaluation settings. The rows differ in evaluated subsets and inference protocols. Oracle pass@88 measures whether a correct candidate exists, whereas best-of-1616 reports a selected candidate under a different budget. These values provide context and are not a matched ranking.

A.6 A worked example of the mutation-verifier reward

The reward of Section 2.3 is clearest on a single instance. The instance shows how the reward spreads credit across fault classes and how it rewards a group of parallel attempts for covering different edit locations.

The loop on one instance.

The example composites two real rollouts on SWE-bench Verified, matplotlib__matplotlib-21568 and django__django-16950. The task, reproduction, and assertion design (stages 1, 2, 4), the mutant set and kills (stages 3, 5), and the group statistics (stage 6) all come from those runs.

  1. 1.

    The task. An over-restrictive rule rejects an input it should accept, treating a legal separator as illegal. A correct fix broadens the rule to admit the character while still rejecting malformed inputs.

  2. 2.

    Reproduce before editing. The agent writes a minimal script that triggers the reported failure, localizes the defect to the validation routine, and applies a small targeted change. Reproducing first ensures the later test observes the real defect instead of a patch artifact.

  3. 3.

    Adversarial mutation. From the model’s own patch, a fix in one file with eleven changed lines all exercised by the test, the adversary produces eight behavior-changing variants of the fixed region (Table 12). Each is a plausible but subtly wrong rewrite meant to defeat a shallow test, spread across five fault classes so the test must probe several input regimes.

  4. 4.

    The discriminative test. A shallow check that only confirms the reported input no longer errors catches at most one variant and earns near-zero reward. The objective instead drives the policy to assert concrete required outputs on inputs chosen to separate each fault class, so every wrong variant fails an assertion.

  5. 5.

    The mutation gauntlet. Each variant runs against the test and counts as eliminated only when an assertion fails, so a crash gives no credit. The loop repeats until no variant survives or the budget is spent. Here the test reaches the fixpoint across all five fault classes (Table 12), so assertion credit spreads across classes and the fixpoint gates the correctness reward.

  6. 6.

    Edit-location diversity. The four parallel attempts stay spread across locations on django__django-16950. Three edited the consensus forms module (forms/models.py), including the selected verified attempt, and the fourth edited an upstream model-field module (fields/__init__.py). The edit term credits both a plausible or validated location and an edit distinct from the group, so the objective rewards covering the space and staying diverse.

DeepSWE’s binary grader resolves zero tasks for either policy, so we score partial credit against its fail-to-pass tests.

We record the protocol behind Table 5 here.

Exposure split.

Table 5a separates training issues, test issues from training repositories, and test issues from repositories excluded from training. Section 3.1 defines training exposure.

Reward controls.

B.2 Generator and verifier swap

This experiment separates the two things training changed. Repair generation and candidate selection are held in fixed roles, and each is swapped independently between the base and trained policies, so the four cells of Table 15 span every combination at one attempt budget. Holding the generator at base and replacing only the verifier raises end-to-end resolution from 31.9%31.9\% to 36.5%36.5\% and selection accuracy from 52.0%52.0\% to 66.0%66.0\%, which shows the verifier changes which patch is returned rather than which patches exist. Holding the verifier at base and replacing only the generator reaches 38.5%38.5\%, so both roles contribute on their own. The interaction term is the diagonal contrast, (43.0−38.5)−(36.5−31.9)=−0.1(43.0-38.5)-(36.5-31.9)=-0.1 points with a 95%95\% interval of [−2.6,2.4][-2.6,2.4], so the two contributions add rather than multiply and neither is a precondition for the other paying off.

B.3 Cross-error-source transfer

A verifier trained against one family of incorrect programs may only have learned that family. Table 16 moves the error source progressively away from training while holding the evaluation bank and the issues fixed, so any decline isolates distribution shift in the negatives rather than a change in difficulty. Rejection falls monotonically for every policy, and for the RL verifier it runs 91.0%91.0\% on familiar operators, 84.0%84.0\% on held-out operators, 79.0%79.0\% on variants from an excluded generator, and 74.0%74.0\% on natural incorrect repairs written by independent systems. The decline is gradual rather than a collapse, and the margin over SFT stays near constant at 1111 to 1212 points across all four sources, which indicates the objective taught discrimination that outlives its training operators. The last row is the one that matters for deployment, since those repairs were produced the way a real candidate would be, and correct-alternative acceptance holds at 78.0%78.0\% there, so the verifier is not buying rejection by refusing everything.

B.7 Assertion-credit ablation

The unsigned kill credit of Eq. 4 pays an assertion only for detecting a wrong variant. The signed two-sided rule also charges it for rejecting a gold-labeled correct alternative (Table 18).

The signed variant is evaluated in this ablation. All other results use unsigned assertion credit. The improvements in this table do not establish the signed variant’s performance on the transfer benchmarks.

B.8 Weighted supervised fine-tuning ablation

Table 19 asks whether weighting the corpus matters or whether any fine-tuning on the same trajectories would do. All variants see the same data under the same token budget, so only the weight assigned to each example changes. Resolution and localization diversity rise together as terms are added, from 33.7%33.7\% and 1.551.55 under uniform weights to 35.2%35.2\% and 1.981.98 with the full weighting, and the exploration term is where the diversity gain concentrates. The interface-compliance control is the informative row. It repairs formatting and tool-call handling without exposing any task solution, and it reaches 32.6%32.6\% with 1.451.45 distinct localizations, below uniform weighting on both, so the gain is not the model merely learning to survive the scaffold. Because the corpus is fixed across rows, these differences are attributable to the weighting rule rather than to data selection.

B.9 Operational metric definitions

Section 3.1 defines repair accuracy, candidate coverage, selection efficiency, and patch-level verifier metrics. The generated eight-candidate sets and frozen verifier banks are different populations. Acceptance coverage is the fraction of issues with at least one accepted candidate. Selection accuracy is the fraction whose selected candidate is correct. Correct-alternative acceptance is the fraction of gold-labeled correct alternatives accepted by the test. Cross-generator rejection is measured on natural incorrect repairs from independent generators, as in Table 16.

For a candidate set 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k}, coverage is Ck=Pr(∃P∈𝒞k:𝒢(P)=1)C_{k}=\Pr(\exists P\in\mathcal{C}_{k}:\mathcal{G}(P)=1). If AkA_{k} is the probability that the selector returns a correct member of that set, selection efficiency is Qk=Ak/CkQ_{k}=A_{k}/C_{k} for Ck>0C_{k}>0. The zero-survivor rate is the fraction of instances whose tests detect every scored mutant at the stated audit size. Distinct localizations count unique edited locations across attempts, with empty patches contributing no location.

B.10 Supervised-fine-tuning weighting ablation

Table B.10 isolates the exploration factor of Eq. 1 by setting λ=0\lambda=0 while leaving the quality tiers and the efficiency factor in place. It also reports plain rejection-sampling fine-tuning, which keeps only gold-resolved trajectories and is the standard alternative to a weighted corpus. Rejection sampling already improves on uniform weighting, so part of the gain is simply preferring successful trajectories. Turning the exploration factor on adds the rest, raising distinct localizations from 1.741.74 to 1.981.98 on Verified and from 3.703.70 to 4.134.13 on SWE-PolyBench with matching resolution gains on both suites. Reporting two suites matters here, because a diversity gain confined to the training benchmark would suggest the weighting had fit the corpus rather than taught a search behavior.

The λ=0\lambda{=}0 row removes only the exploration factor of Eq. 1, isolating its effect on diversity.

B.13 The Eight Methodology Preambles

One of the preambles below, prepended to the base system prompt, conditions each of the eight parallel chains in the methodology-diversity arm, so the chains differ by conditioning rather than by temperature. We give the eight in canonical order, lightly edited for space.

B.14 Reactive Location-Ban Logic

The reactive arms walk the candidate grid sequentially, grouping cells by location in confidence order, and let the verifier steer subsequent attempts.

Ban, freeze, early-stop.

Three rules govern each cell. Ban on confirmed fail. The walk bans a location proven wrong, skips its remaining approaches, and moves to a new site. Freeze site, vary edit. A weak pass means the site is plausibly right and the edit is wrong, so the walk keeps the location and varies the approach. Early stop. The walk stops on the first strong pass.

The walk enforces bans by filtering, holding banned location keys in a set and skipping any cell whose location is in that set.

A second guard gates the ban on the edit being real and on-plan, since a cell that drifted off its assigned file never tested that location and must not ban it. The localization-ban configuration uses the explicit “look elsewhere” prompt below.

B.15 Experiment Configurations

The three meanings of k=8k{=}8.

All three test-time axes use k=8k{=}8 and mean something different by it. For pass@8, eight attempts run with sample 1 greedy and samples 2 to 8 at T=0.7T{=}0.7. The samples are independent but not identically distributed, since the greedy sample comes from a different distribution than the temperature ones, and diversity comes only from temperature. For the eight methodologies, eight parallel chains each take a distinct methodology preamble (Appendix B.13), so diversity comes from conditioning and the chains explore different solution axes. For the coverage-space arms, eight candidate cells per instance differ in how diversity is enforced and how candidates are verified, which isolates grid conditioning from the reactive verifier.
